components.name: Broker
components.helpText:
Brokers enrich the contents of the existing message with additional data or structure in a number of different ways.

Request-response brokers can make calls to other systems such as a database or HTTP(s) RESTful services. Aggregating brokers consume incoming messages until a condition is met, for example after every 10 messages. Resequencing brokers consume incoming messages until a condition is met, then release them as a list of newly ordered events. This can provide a powerful function when combined with a Splitter as the next component.

components.name: Default List Splitter
components.helpText:
Splitters typically take in a single payload and split it into a number of smaller payloads that are sent to the downstream consumer one by one.

A ready-made, no-code splitter for the common case where the incoming payload is already a java.util.List. It performs no transformation; it unwraps the list into one message per item.

  • Input: A single payload that is itself a list of 1 to n objects
  • Output: 1 to n separate messages, each message containing one of the objects from that list, in the same order
Input  Output 
MessagePayload MessagePayload
1“AA”, “BB”, “CC” 1“AA”
   2“BB”
   3“CC”

If you need to derive the split items rather than just unwrap an existing list (for example, splitting a String on a delimiter, or splitting one object into several different objects), use the Splitter component instead; it lets you write that logic yourself.

properties.name: host
properties.helpText:
The host attribute is the hostname or IP address the module advertises to the Dashboard. Defaults to localhost if left unset:

  1. public.service.address — externally advertised hostname (e.g. behind a proxy)
  2. server.address — Spring Boot’s bind address
  3. Defaults to “localhost” if neither is set

So for a deployed module reachable at a real hostname:

public.service.address=my-module.example.com

properties.name: port
properties.helpText:
The port attribute is the HTTP port number the module is listening on — used by the Dashboard to construct the module’s REST URL.

It is resolved in this order:

  1. public.service.port — the externally advertised port (useful behind a reverse proxy/load balancer)
  2. server.port — Spring Boot’s own port
  3. Defaults to 8080 if neither is set

So if your module runs internally on port 8443 but is exposed publicly on port 443 via a proxy, you’d set:

public.service.port=443

and the module will advertise port 443 to the Dashboard.

properties.name: protocol
properties.helpText:
This is typically left as default / unset.

The protocol attribute on a Module is the HTTP scheme used to reach the module’s REST endpoint — i.e., “http” or “https”.

Together with host, port, and context, it forms the full base URL of the module so that the Ikasan Dashboard and other services know how to communicate with it.

How it gets set (in ModuleBuilder):

  1. First checks the Spring property public.service.protocol (useful when behind a reverse proxy/load balancer that terminates TLS).
  2. Falls back to server.protocol (Spring Boot’s own SSL setting).
  3. Defaults to “http” if neither is set.

So in practice, if your module is deployed behind HTTPS you’d set:

public.service.protocol=https

and the module will advertise itself as HTTPS to the Dashboard, even if the internal Spring Boot server is still plain HTTP.

components.helpText:
Routers choose which downstream route or routes receive each payload.

Use this router to send a payload to one or more routes, such as both routeA and routeB.

Unlike the Single Recipient Router there is no "default" fallback - the router must always return at least one route name, it can never return zero.

Each matched route runs to completion, in order, before the next one starts. By default, the payload is cloned before being sent down each route (except the last) so routes cannot affect each other by mutating a shared payload.

components.name: Object To XML String Converter
components.helpText:
A Converter accepts a source payload and returns a conversion result. Its source and target types may differ, so use it when the Java type or structure must change. A Translator, by contrast, modifies the supplied payload in place and does not replace it.

Ikasan class: ObjectToXMLStringConverter

Marshals a plain Java object into an XML string using JAXB. The object's class must be JAXB-annotated (or otherwise buildable into a JAXBContext) - any nested/referenced types it needs must be reachable from its own annotations, since only one root class is supplied here.

Note: this expects the payload to already be the plain object, not a raw JMS message - if the upstream component is a JMS consumer, place a JMS Object Message To Object Converter directly before this one to unwrap the ObjectMessage first.

properties.name: trustedObjectPackages
properties.helpText:
Receiving a Java object such as Order? ActiveMQ must be told which Java packages it may read from JMS ObjectMessage bodies. Enter the package, for example org.example.cat.domain (not the Order class name). Separate additional packages with commas.

Leave empty for text, JSON, XML or byte messages. This adds to the default trusted packages; it does not allow all packages. It does not change the message type or create an Order object.

For an ObjectMessage-to-Object converter, keep auto content conversion off on the consumer. Regenerate and restart the module after changing this setting. Uses standard ActiveMQ Classic JNDI, or a directly supplied ActiveMQ connection factory. For a custom JNDI properties map/provider or a wrapped factory, configure trust in that custom factory instead.
properties.validationMessage: Enter comma-separated Java package names, e.g. org.example.cat.domain. Wildcards (*) are not allowed.

components.name: Translator
components.helpText:
A Translator modifies the supplied payload in place and does not replace it, so its Java type remains the same. A Converter, by contrast, returns a conversion result and may change the Java type or structure.

Implement the required in-place transformation in the generated translator class. The payload type must be mutable.
components.implementationGuidance: Inspect the generated user/ implementation. A class may be only a stub; a recipe may supply behaviour. Complete and test it within the requested scope, preserving existing developer logic.
completionChecks: Trace a representative input through the component and test the expected output or side effect, including a relevant failure case.
Locate the generated user/ class and inspect its method bodies. Complete throwing, empty or no-op scaffolds within the requested scope; preserve existing developer logic.
Perform and test the intended in-place mutation of a mutable payload. Use a Converter for replacement values.
Verify required beans and external resources independently of compilation. Report runtime delivery as unverified until exercised.
